title: A hanging chain is not a parabola, and flipping its curve gives the perfect arch

cover.alt: The stainless-steel Gateway Arch in St. Louis rising against a blue sky.

body: Let a chain hang from two points and it settles into a **catenary**, from the Latin *catena*, chain. It looks like a parabola but is not one: Joachim Jungius proved the difference, in work published in 1669, and Leibniz, Huygens and Johann Bernoulli found the exact equation in 1691. A hanging chain carries only tension, so turning its curve upside down gives an arch that carries only compression, the ideal shape for a free-standing arch of constant thickness. Robert Hooke worked this out in 1675 but hid it in a Latin anagram, decoded after his death in 1705: as hangs a flexible cable, so, inverted, stand the touching pieces of an arch.

slides.alt: A metal chain hanging between two fixed points, sagging in a smooth U-shaped curve.
slides.caption: A chain hanging under its own weight. Galileo wrote in 1638 that the curve is only approximately a parabola.

left.label: Parabola
left.text: The curve of a thrown ball, or of a bridge cable carrying a heavy, evenly spread roadway. Galileo thought a chain hung this way.

right.label: Catenary
right.text: The curve of a chain carrying only its own weight. Its equation uses the hyperbolic cosine: y = a cosh(x/a). Joachim Jungius proved it is a different curve.

slides.heading: Why the upside-down chain makes a perfect arch

steps.label: A hanging chain feels pure tension
No bending: the arch stands by itself

slides.heading: The Gateway Arch
slides.text: The [Gateway Arch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gateway_Arch) in St. Louis is 192 m tall and 192 m wide. It is often called an inverted catenary, but its legs are heavier than its top, so it follows a weighted catenary: the curve of a chain with lighter links in the middle. It can sway up to 46 cm in high wind.

events.text: Galileo: a hanging cord is roughly a parabola
Jungius's proof that it is not one is published
Robert Hooke hides the arch principle in an anagram
Leibniz, Huygens and Bernoulli derive the equation

slides.question: Why does an inverted catenary make such a good arch?
options: Its stones are only squeezed, never bent
It is the lightest possible curve
slides.explanation: A hanging chain carries only tension. Flip it and every force becomes compression along the curve, so a free-standing arch of that shape has no bending to resist.
